title: Mock paper
intro:
**2 hours · 100 marks · 4 questions of 25 marks · answer all.** Closed book; an approved calculator only. Derivations are needed only where asked.

Work on paper. When you submit (or time runs out) every part shows a **worked answer** and a **mark scheme** - tick the points your answer contains to get your score.

Covers the whole syllabus in the same shape as the 2024 and 2025 papers: optimality and feasible sets, least norm and transformations, a KKT production problem, and algorithms (descent, barrier, cross-entropy).

sections.title: Answer ALL questions
sections.blurb: Four questions, 25 marks each. Calculator allowed; closed book.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For $f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3 + 4x^2$ on $-1 \le x \le 3$: find every critical point, classify each, and state the global maximum and minimum on the interval.
parts.answer:
$f(x) = x^2(x - 2)^2$, $f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 + 8x = 4x(x - 1)(x - 2)$ → critical points $x = 0, 1, 2$.
$f''(x) = 12x^2 - 24x + 8$: $f''(0) = 8 > 0$, $f''(1) = -4 < 0$, $f''(2) = 8 > 0$.

| x | f | Type |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | local minimum - and **global minimum** |
| 1 | 1 | **local maximum** (not global) |
| 2 | 0 | local minimum - and **global minimum** (tied with x = 0) |
| −1 (end) | 9 | **global maximum** (tied) |
| 3 (end) | 9 | **global maximum** (tied) |

The global maximum is at the end points, which are not critical points - always evaluate them on a closed interval.

points.text: End values 9 → global max; 0 and 2 global min

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
Consider $\min (x_1 - 3)^2 + (x_2 - 3)^2$ s.t. $x_1 + x_2 \le 4$, $x_2 \le 3$, $x_1 \ge 0$, $x_2 \ge 0$.
(i) Sketch the feasible region with level curves of $f$. **[4]** (ii) Find the solution and verify it with the KKT conditions. **[5]** (iii) If the objective is changed to $\max\ x_1 + 2x_2$ on the same region, find the solution graphically. **[3]**
parts.answer:
**(i)** Region: the quadrilateral with vertices **(0, 0), (4, 0), (1, 3), (0, 3)** - below $x_1 + x_2 = 4$ and $x_2 = 3$. Level sets of $f$ are circles centred at (3, 3), which is infeasible ($3 + 3 > 4$).

![Feasible region, level circles and both optima](/notes-files/cse/sem7/en3330-mock1-ans-q1b.png)

**(ii)** The closest feasible point to (3, 3) is its projection onto $x_1 + x_2 = 4$: $(3, 3) - \tfrac{6 - 4}{2}(1, 1) = \mathbf{(2, 2)}$, $f^* = 2$.
KKT with only $g_1 = x_1 + x_2 - 4$ active: $\nabla f + \mu_1\nabla g_1 = (2(2 - 3), 2(2 - 3)) + \mu_1(1, 1) = 0 \Rightarrow \mu_1 = 2 \ge 0$ ✓. Other multipliers 0 ($x_2 = 2 < 3$, $x > 0$ - inactive) ✓; complementary slackness ✓; primal feasible ✓. Convex problem ⇒ global minimum.

**(iii)** Level lines $x_1 + 2x_2 = c$ have slope −1/2; push them up-right. Vertex values: (0, 0) → 0, (4, 0) → 4, (1, 3) → **7**, (0, 3) → 6. Solution **(1, 3)**, value 7 - an LP optimum is at a vertex.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find and classify the critical points of $f(\mathbf{x}) = x_1^3 + x_2^3 - 3x_1x_2$.
parts.answer:
$\nabla f = [3x_1^2 - 3x_2,\ 3x_2^2 - 3x_1]^T = 0 \Rightarrow x_2 = x_1^2$ and $x_1 = x_2^2 = x_1^4 \Rightarrow x_1(x_1^3 - 1) = 0$. Real solutions: **(0, 0)** and **(1, 1)**.

$\nabla^2 f = \begin{bmatrix}6x_1 & -3\\ -3 & 6x_2\end{bmatrix}$.
- (0, 0): $\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3\\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, eigenvalues ±3 → indefinite → **saddle**, $f = 0$.
- (1, 1): $\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3\\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}$, eigenvalues 3, 9 → positive definite → **strict local minimum**, $f = -1$. Not global ($f \to -\infty$ along $x_1 = x_2 \to -\infty$).

questions.explain: Every "classify" part is: gradient = 0, then the Hessian sign at each point. Write the eigenvalues - "the Hessian is positive" earns nothing.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the point on the plane $x_1 + 2x_2 + 2x_3 = 9$ closest to the origin (i) with a Lagrange multiplier **[5]** and (ii) geometrically **[3]**, and give the minimum distance.
parts.answer:
**(i)** $\min \|\mathbf{x}\|^2$ s.t. $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x} = 9$, $\mathbf{a} = (1, 2, 2)$. $\mathcal L = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x} + 
u(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x} - 9)$; $
abla_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal L = 2\mathbf{x} + 
u\mathbf{a} = 0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{x} = -	frac{
u}{2}\mathbf{a}$. Substitute: $-	frac{
u}{2}\|\mathbf{a}\|^2 = 9$, $\|\mathbf{a}\|^2 = 9 \Rightarrow 
u = -2$, $\mathbf{x}^* = (1, 2, 2)$.

**(ii)** The closest point is the foot of the normal from the origin: $\mathbf{x}^* = 	frac{9}{\|\mathbf{a}\|^2}\mathbf{a} = (1, 2, 2)$.

Distance $\|\mathbf{x}^*\| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$ (= $|9|/\|\mathbf{a}\|$).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Fit $y = c_0 + c_1x$ to the points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 4) by least squares: write the problem as $\min\|A\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{y}\|^2$, derive the normal equations, and solve.
parts.answer:
$A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\ 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\3\\4\end{bmatrix}$. $F(\mathbf{c}) = \|A\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{y}\|^2$, $\nabla F = 2A^T(A\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{y}) = 0 \Rightarrow A^TA\mathbf{c} = A^T\mathbf{y}$ (normal equations). $\nabla^2F = 2A^TA \succ 0$ (columns independent) ⇒ unique global minimum.
$$A^TA = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 3\\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix},\quad A^T\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}8\\11\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \mathbf{c} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -3\\ -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8\\11\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}7/6\\ 3/2\end{bmatrix}.$$
Line $y = 1.167 + 1.5x$; residuals (−1/6, 1/3, −1/6) sum to zero, as they must with an intercept.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A variable must satisfy $2 \le x \le 10$. (i) Give a $\tanh$ transformation that removes the bounds and the chain-rule expression for $dF/dz$. **[4]** (ii) For $f(x) = (x - 12)^2$, explain what gradient descent on $z$ does, and propose a transformation that fixes it. **[4]**
parts.answer:
**(i)** $x = 6 + 4\tanh z$ maps $z \in \mathbb{R}$ onto $(2, 10)$. With $F(z) = f(6 + 4\tanh z)$:
$$\frac{dF}{dz} = f'(x)\,\frac{dx}{dz} = f'(x)\cdot 4(1 - \tanh^2 z).$$

**(ii)** The constrained optimum is the bound $x = 10$ (closest to 12). $f'(x) = 2(x - 12) < 0$ on the interval, so $dF/dz < 0$ always and descent pushes $z \to +\infty$: $x$ creeps towards 10 but never reaches it, and the factor $1 - \tanh^2 z \to 0$ makes progress vanish - **no finite minimiser**.
Fix: a map whose range is the **closed** interval, e.g. $x = 6 + 4\sin z$ (bound reached at $z = \pi/2$, where $dF/dz = 0$) or $x = 6 + 4\cdot\tfrac{2z}{1 + z^2}$ (reached at $z = 1$).

points.text: Optimum at bound; z → ∞, vanishing gradient

questions.explain: Part (c) shows why the choice of transformation matters: tanh is smooth and one-to-one, but cannot represent a solution that sits on a bound.

questions.prompt:
Question 3. A workshop builds three drone models P, Q and R ($x_P, x_Q, x_R$ units per month).
- Assembly: P needs 2 hours, Q needs 1 hour and R needs 3 hours. 200 assembly hours are available and **all** must be used.
- Testing: P needs 1 hour, Q needs 2 hours, R needs 1 hour. 150 test hours are available and **all** must be used.
- Parts cost Rs 10 000 for P, Rs 8 000 for Q and Rs 20 000 for R; the parts budget is Rs 1.22 million.
- Profit (thousand Rs) is $50x_P + 40x_Q + 120x_R - x_R^2$ - R's profit falls as the market saturates.

parts.label: i
parts.answer:
Working in thousands of rupees:
$$\begin{aligned} \max\quad & P = 50x_P + 40x_Q + 120x_R - x_R^2\\ \text{s.t.}\quad & 2x_P + x_Q + 3x_R = 200 && \text{(assembly)}\\ & x_P + 2x_Q + x_R = 150 && \text{(testing)}\\ & 10x_P + 8x_Q + 20x_R \le 1220 && \text{(budget)}\\ & x_P, x_Q, x_R \ge 0. \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: ii
parts.prompt: Write the Lagrangian and the KKT conditions.
parts.answer:
Minimise $f = -P$. With $h_1 = 2x_P + x_Q + 3x_R - 200$, $h_2 = x_P + 2x_Q + x_R - 150$, $g = 10x_P + 8x_Q + 20x_R - 1220$:
$$\mathcal L = -(50x_P + 40x_Q + 120x_R - x_R^2) + \lambda_1h_1 + \lambda_2h_2 + \mu g.$$
Stationarity: $-50 + 2\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + 10\mu = 0$; $\ -40 + \lambda_1 + 2\lambda_2 + 8\mu = 0$; $\ -(120 - 2x_R) + 3\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + 20\mu = 0$.
Primal: $h_1 = h_2 = 0$, $g \le 0$. Dual: $\mu \ge 0$. Complementary slackness: $\mu g = 0$.

parts.label: iii
parts.prompt: Solve with the KKT conditions. Report the plan, the profit and the multipliers.
parts.answer:
**Reduce with the equalities.** From testing, $x_P = 150 - 2x_Q - x_R$; into assembly: $-3x_Q + x_R = -100$, so
$$x_Q = \frac{100 + x_R}{3},\qquad x_P = \frac{250 - 5x_R}{3}.$$
Profit on this line: $P = 5500 + 50x_R - x_R^2$ (concave, unconstrained peak at $x_R = 25$). Budget: $1100 + 6x_R \le 1220 \Rightarrow x_R \le 20$.

**Case μ = 0:** stationarity gives $x_R = 25$ - budget $1250 > 1220$: **infeasible**, reject.

**Case μ > 0 (budget active):** $x_R = 20$, $x_P = 50$, $x_Q = 40$. Stationarity with $120 - 2x_R = 80$:
$2\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + 10\mu = 50$, $\lambda_1 + 2\lambda_2 + 8\mu = 40$, $3\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + 20\mu = 80$ ⇒ $\lambda_1 = 13.33$, $\lambda_2 = 6.67$, $\mu = 5/3 \ge 0$ ✓.

**Plan:** $x_P = 50$, $x_Q = 40$, $x_R = 20$ (whole numbers - no rounding needed), $P = 6100$ thousand Rs = **Rs 6.1 million**. Check: assembly 100 + 40 + 60 = 200 ✓, testing 50 + 80 + 20 = 150 ✓, budget 500 + 320 + 400 = 1220 ✓.

parts.label: iv
parts.prompt: Interpret $\mu$. Would raising the budget by Rs 60 000 be worth it if the extra money cost Rs 80 000 in interest?
parts.answer: $\mu = 5/3$ is the **shadow price** of the budget: each extra thousand rupees of budget raises the optimal profit by about Rs 1 667. Rs 60 000 more ($x_R$ could reach 30, but the unconstrained peak is 25, reached at a budget of 1250) - so only Rs 30 000 is usable: $x_R = 25$, $P = 6125$, a gain of **Rs 25 000** (μ is a local rate, so 60 × 5/3 = 100 overstates it). That is less than Rs 80 000 of interest - **not worth it**.

questions.explain: When the objective is concave in a maximisation, first find the unconstrained peak - if it is infeasible, the budget is active and μ > 0 tells you by how much it binds.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For $f(\mathbf{x}) = x_1^2 + 5x_2^2$ from $\mathbf{x}^{(0)} = (5, 1)$: (i) take one steepest-descent step with **exact line search** **[5]**; (ii) take one Newton step and compare **[3]**.
parts.answer:
**(i)** $\nabla f = (2x_1, 10x_2) = (10, 10)$, $H = \mathrm{diag}(2, 10)$, $f(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}) = 30$. For a quadratic the exact step along $-\mathbf{g}$ is
$$\alpha^* = \frac{\mathbf{g}^T\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{g}^TH\mathbf{g}} = \frac{200}{200 + 1000} = \frac16.$$
$\mathbf{x}^{(1)} = (5, 1) - \tfrac16(10, 10) = (3.333, -0.667)$, $f = 11.11 + 2.22 = 13.33$. (The next gradient $(6.67, -6.67)$ is orthogonal to the previous one - the zig-zag of steepest descent.)

**(ii)** $\mathbf{x}^{(1)} = \mathbf{x}^{(0)} - H^{-1}\mathbf{g} = (5, 1) - (5, 1) = (0, 0)$, $f = 0$ - the exact minimum in **one** step, because Newton's quadratic model of a quadratic is exact. Steepest descent needs many steps (condition number 5); Newton costs a Hessian solve per step.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
Solve $\min x_1 + x_2$ s.t. $x_1 \ge 1$, $x_2 \ge 2$ with the log-barrier method $\phi_t(\mathbf{x}) = x_1 + x_2 - \tfrac1t[\ln(x_1 - 1) + \ln(x_2 - 2)]$.
(i) Find the central path $\mathbf{x}(t)$. **[4]** (ii) Show the duality gap is $2/t$ and find $t$ for a gap ≤ $10^{-3}$. **[2]** (iii) Contrast with a quadratic penalty. **[2]**
parts.answer:
**(i)** $\partial\phi_t/\partial x_1 = 1 - \dfrac{1}{t(x_1 - 1)} = 0 \Rightarrow x_1 = 1 + \dfrac1t$; similarly $x_2 = 2 + \dfrac1t$. ($\nabla^2\phi_t \succ 0$ - a minimum.) As $t \to \infty$, $\mathbf{x}(t) \to (1, 2)$, $f^* = 3$.

**(ii)** $f(\mathbf{x}(t)) - f^* = 2/t$ (= $m/t$ with $m = 2$ constraints). $2/t \le 10^{-3} \Rightarrow t \ge 2000$.

**(iii)** The barrier keeps every iterate **strictly feasible** (approaches from inside, needs a feasible start, handles inequalities only). The quadratic penalty approaches from **outside** - iterates are infeasible until $\rho \to \infty$ - but can start anywhere and handles equalities. Both become ill-conditioned as $t$ or $\rho$ grows.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt:
The cross-entropy method **minimises** $f(\mathbf{x}) = (x_1 - 2)^2 + (x_2 + 1)^2$ with 3 elites. The samples are:

| i | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $x_1$ | 1 | 3 | 0 | 4 | 2 | 2 |
| $x_2$ | 0 | −2 | 1 | 0 | −3 | 0 |

(i) Identify the elites. **[2]** (ii) Compute the next mean and covariance. **[6]** (iii) Why might the covariance need a floor? **[1]**
parts.answer:
**(i)** $f$: 2, 2, 8, 5, 4, 1. Smallest three: **sample 6 (1), samples 1 and 2 (2 each)** → elites (2, 0), (1, 0), (3, −2).

**(ii)** $\boldsymbol\mu = \tfrac13(2 + 1 + 3,\ 0 + 0 - 2) = (2,\ -2/3)$.
Deviations: (0, 2/3), (−1, 2/3), (1, −4/3).
$$\Sigma = \frac13\sum(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu)^T = \frac13\begin{bmatrix}0 + 1 + 1 & 0 - \tfrac23 - \tfrac43\\ \cdot & \tfrac49 + \tfrac49 + \tfrac{16}9\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0.667 & -0.667\\ -0.667 & 0.889\end{bmatrix}.$$
The mean has moved toward the true minimiser (2, −1).

**(iii)** With few elites the covariance shrinks fast and can collapse before reaching the optimum (premature convergence) - adding a small $\epsilon I$ keeps exploring.

questions.explain: For exact line search on a quadratic, use α = gᵀg / gᵀHg directly - deriving it from d/dα f(x − αg) = 0 also earns the marks.
